title: Facing prejudice
hookLine: meeting hostility with dignity and courage
tomorrow: Simran has to tell her side at school. what about the fear?

lines: A POET NAMES WHAT THEY MOCKED.
cards: By lunch, an account with no face has left a comment under Simran's bus stop video: go back home. She was born two towns over. Her thumbs are already typing something she'd regret.
Then a text from her dad, Harjit, who hears worse at truck stops: before you answer, read Ang 1293. So she does, and finds something odd.
Right there in the Guru Granth Sahib, a poet tells everyone the exact thing people used to look down on him for. He doesn't hide it. He puts it in a hymn.
Why would anyone write the insult into scripture?

teach.b: The poet is Bhagat Ravidas. In Sikh tradition he was a leatherworker, born into a family others of his time treated as untouchable. His hymns sit in the Guru Granth Sahib beside the Gurus' own.

On Ang 1293 he says, in paraphrase: my people carried dead cattle around Benares every day. Now even the leading Brahmins bow to them, because Ravidas has taken shelter in your Name. So here's the puzzle solved.
He doesn't argue with the label, and he doesn't shrink from it either.
He says it plainly, in the open, and then stands on something the label can't touch: the Name.
That's dignity. Not pretending the word didn't land. Not snarling back.

Just refusing to let someone else's word decide who you are. The detail to tell a friend tonight: a man people wouldn't share a well with is sung in gurdwaras, in his own words. Harjit's version is smaller.
At a fuel stop once, a man told him to go home. Harjit smiled and said: I am home.
Simran deletes her version. She types three words under the video, I am home, and puts the phone face down.

how: Sikhs sing the hymns of Bhagat Ravidas along with the Gurus' hymns in the gurdwara, and some Sikhs point to them when talking about caste and prejudice.

o: staying quiet so that nobody gets upset with you
meeting hostility with dignity, not shrinking or snarling
proving them wrong by being twice as loud as they were

games.q: the puzzle, piece by piece — tap the pairs.

s: Ravidas was one of the ten Sikh Gurus
he was a bhagat, a saint-poet whose hymns sit in the Guru Granth Sahib beside the Gurus' own.
dignity means acting like the insult didn't hurt
Ravidas names the label plainly; dignity is not letting it decide who you are.
a hymn in the Guru Granth Sahib names the poet's own people and their work
Ang 1293: my people carried dead cattle around Benares.

games.q: at your part-time job, a customer mispronounces your name on purpose and laughs. going by today, what fits best?
o: say your name once, clearly and kindly, and carry on serving.
laugh along and tell them a nickname so it's easier for everyone.
say nothing now, then post about them in a review later.
games.why: Ravidas says plainly who he is and stands on something deeper. no shrinking, no snarling: dignity.

practice: Sit or stand tall: feet flat, shoulders down, chin level, hands open. Let one label someone once put on you come to mind, and keep the posture anyway. With each slow breath, let the word be there without letting it bend your spine.

wordCard.voice: Facing prejudice. Meeting hostility with dignity: saying who you are plainly, and standing on something their words can't reach.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: Ravidas, the bhagat whose hymn on Ang 1293 names his own people's work.

carryVoice: The line for today: dignity, the way Ravidas named his people and stood on the Name. Three words under a video, and the phone face down.

sources.ref: Ang 1293, Raag Malar, Bhagat Ravidas ('meri jaat kutbaandhla dhor dhovanta nitah baanaarasi aas paasa'), paraphrased
